--- title: "CMIP6 SST post-processing: validation of the 2026 ensemble refresh" subtitle: Regridding error, drift and anomaly checks for `cmorph-pp` 2026.11 author: - name: Astrid Lindqvist orcid: 0000-0002-1825-0097 email: a.lindqvist@northfield.ac.uk affiliations: - ref: nfld - name: "Tomás Ferreira-Okoye" affiliations: [ {ref: nfld}, {ref: hadley} ] affiliations: - id: nfld name: University of Northfield department: Dept. of Earth System Science - id: hadley name: Met Office Hadley Centre date: 2026-11-12 date-modified: last-modified abstract: | We validate step 2 of `cmorph-pp`, which regrids monthly CMIP6 sea-surface temperature (`tos`) from five models to a common 1° grid and converts it to anomalies. Conservative regridding changes the global-mean SST by less than 0.004 K in every model. Two models drift by more than our 0.1 K/century threshold in their control runs and are de-drifted before use. keywords: [CMIP6, sea surface temperature, regridding, xESMF,model drift] bibliography: references.bib csl: american-meteorological-society.csl lang: en-GB format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true code-fold: true html-math-method: katex fig-format: svg pdf: documentclass: scrartcl papersize: a4 geometry: - margin=2.5cm include-in-header: text: | \usepackage{siunitx} execute: echo: false warning: false cache: true jupyter: python3 crossref: eq-prefix: Eq. fig-prefix: Fig. --- {{< include _common.qmd >}} ## Summary {#sec-summary} ::: {.callout-important} ## Bottom line The regridded ensemble is fit for the detection-and-attribution work in WP3. Regridding changes the global-mean SST by **< 0.004 K** for every model (@tbl-regrid-error), the anomaly time series agree with the native-grid ones to within 0.01 K at every time step, and only `CanESM5` and `IPSL-CM6A-LR` need de-drifting (@sec-drift). ::: ## Data and models {#sec-data} We use monthly `tos` from the `historical` (1850–2014) and `ssp245`/`ssp585` (2015–2100) experiments of the five models in @tbl-models, three members each where available [@eyring2016; @oneill2016scenariomip]. Observations are HadISST [@rayner2003hadisst] and OISST v2.1 [@huang2021oisst, pp. 2923--2939], on their native $1^\circ$ and $0.25^\circ$ grids respectively. | Model | Ocean component | Native grid | Members | Ref. | |:--|:--|--:|:-:|---| | CanESM5 | NEMO3.4.1 (ORCA1) | ~1° | 3 | @swart2019canesm5 | | MPI-ESM1-2-HR | MPIOM1.63 (TP04) | 0.4° | 3 | @mueller2018mpiesm | | IPSL-CM6A-LR | NEMO-OPA (eORCA1) | ~1° | 3 | @boucher2020ipsl | | UKESM1-0-LL | NEMO3.6 (eORCA1) | ~1° | 2 | @sellar2019ukesm | | GFDL-CM4 | MOM6 | 0.25° | 1 | @held2019gfdlcm4 | : CMIP6 models in the ensemble refresh. "Members" counts realisations with complete historical *and* scenario output on our ESGF mirror as of 1 November 2026. {#tbl-models} ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-pipeline %%| fig-cap: The cmorph-pp chain. This report covers step 2 only. flowchart LR A[ESGF mirror
native tos] --> B(step 1: CMOR checks) B --> C(step 2: regrid + anomalies) C --> D[(THREDDS)] C --> E(step 3: bias correction) ``` ## Methods {#sec-methods} ### Regridding Fields are regridded with xESMF [@zhuang2023xesmf] using first-order conservative remapping, normalised by the unmasked fraction of each target cell (`conservative_normed`). For a target cell $k$ that overlaps source cells $i$ with overlap areas $a_{ik}$ and ocean mask $m_i \in \{0, 1\}$, $$ \hat T_k = \frac{\sum_i a_{ik}\, m_i\, T_i}{\sum_i a_{ik}\, m_i}, $$ {#eq-conservative} which, unlike plain conservative remapping, does not pull coastal cells towards zero. The global integral $\sum_k A_k \hat T_k$ is conserved exactly only if no target cell is partially masked; the residual error is what @tbl-regrid-error quantifies. ### Anomalies and drift {#sec-drift} Anomalies are taken relative to each member's 1981–2010 monthly climatology (@eq-anomaly). Drift is estimated from the parallel `piControl` segment with a least-squares quadratic fit $d(t) = a + b\,t + c\,t^2$ and subtracted when $|b| > 0.1\,\mathrm{K\,century^{-1}}$^[We tried a linear fit first. It under-corrects `IPSL-CM6A-LR`, whose drift slows down after ~200 years of spin-up.]. $$ T'(y, m) = T(y, m) - \frac{1}{30} \sum_{y'=1981}^{2010} T(y', m) $$ {#eq-anomaly} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} All runs were done on larch[^larch] as one Slurm array, one task per model and experiment: ```{.bash filename="jobs/submit_step2.sh"} sbatch --array=0-14%5 --partition=short --cpus-per-task=32 --mem=120G \ --time=04:00:00 --job-name=pp-step2 jobs/step2.sbatch ``` ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} > Weights for the 0.25° GFDL grid took 19 min to build on 32 cores; every later run reused them from `$CMORPH_WEIGHTS`. ::: :::: [^larch]: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 per node, 768 GB RAM. Regridding is memory-bound, so we used 32 of the 192 cores per task and packed six tasks onto each node. ## Results ### Regridding error ```{python} #| label: tbl-regrid-error #| tbl-cap: "Difference in 1981–2010 global-mean SST (K), regridded minus native, per model. Negative values mean the regridded field is cooler." import pandas as pd err = pd.read_parquet("results/regrid_error.parquet") err.style.format("{:+.4f}").background_gradient(cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.005, vmax=0.005) ``` ```{python} #| label: fig-gmsst #| fig-cap: Global-mean SST anomaly relative to 1981–2010, ensemble mean ± 1σ. #| fig-subcap: #| - "Native grids" #| - Regridded to 1° #| layout-ncol: 2 #| fig-width: 6 #| fig-height: 3.5 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ts = pd.read_parquet("results/gmsst_anom.parquet") for grid in ["native", "1x1"]: fig, ax = plt.subplots() for model, g in ts[ts.grid == grid].groupby("source_id"): ax.plot(g.year, g.anom, lw=0.8, label=model) ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", lw=0.5); ax.set_ylabel("ΔSST (K)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncols=2) plt.show() ``` The two panels of @fig-gmsst are indistinguishable by eye; the largest difference in any annual mean is 0.009 K (`MPI-ESM1-2-HR`, 1883), well below interannual variability. ### Drift +---------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------+ | Model | Drift (K/century) | Action | +===============+===================+==========================================+ | CanESM5 | 0.23 | de-drifted (quadratic fit) | +---------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------+ | IPSL-CM6A-LR | −0.14 | de-drifted; member r3i1p1f1 also has a | | | | step change in 1922, flagged in the QC | +---------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------+ | others | < 0.05 | none | +---------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------+ : Control-run drift and what we did about it. {#tbl-drift} ```{python} #| label: drift-table-raw #| output: asis #| fmt: skip drift = pd.read_csv("results/drift.csv", index_col="source_id") print(drift.to_markdown(floatfmt=("", ".3f", ".3f", ".2e"), tablefmt="pipe")) ``` {{< pagebreak >}} ## Appendix: configuration {.appendix} The exact `cmorph-pp` configuration used for this report (`config/step2.yaml`, commit `4f9c2e1`): ```yaml version: 2026.11.0 regrid: method: conservative_normed grid: {name: 1x1, lon: [-180,180], lat: [-90, 90]} weights_dir: /scratch/cmorph/weights anomaly: reference: [1981,2010] per_member: yes drift: enabled: true models: [CanESM5, IPSL-CM6A-LR] fit: quadratic threshold_K_per_century: 0.1 output: {format: netcdf4, compression: {zlib: true, complevel: 4}} ``` ## References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} :::

Asante" - name: Research Software Engineering, University of Northfield date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%e %B %Y')`" output: bookdown::html_document2: toc: true number_sections: yes fig_caption: true df_print: kable bookdown::pdf_document2: latex_engine: lualatex keep_tex: no bibliography: [refs/krylov.bib, refs/hpc.bib] link-citations: yes params: results: "results/2026-11-03" baseline: "2.4.1" nodes: !r c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) editor_options: markdown: wrap: sentence chunk_output_type: console --- ```{r setup, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=FALSE, fig.align="center", dev="ragg_png", dpi=150} library(data.table) library(ggplot2) knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE) res <- fread(file.path(params$results, "scaling.csv")) ``` # Introduction {#intro} Krylov subspace methods spend most of their time in two kernels: the sparse matrix-vector product (SpMV) and the global reductions needed for inner products and norms. On a few nodes the SpMV dominates, but beyond approx. 16 nodes the reductions become latency-bound, since every `MPI_Allreduce` costs $\mathcal{O}(\log p)$ network hops regardless of message size (cf. the discussion in Ghysels et al. [-@ghysels2013pipelined], Sect. 2). Pipelined GMRES (p-GMRES) hides this latency by overlapping the reduction of iteration $k$ with the SpMV of iteration $k+1$, at the price of extra vector operations and somewhat weaker numerical stability. This note quantifies the trade-off for fernsolve v2.5.0-rc.1 on the larch cluster and compares it with the classical GMRES($m$) implementation in v`r params$baseline`. All timings are medians of 5 runs; the error bars in Fig. \@ref(fig:strong) show the min.–max. range. The test problem is the 3-D convection–diffusion equation $-\nabla\cdot(\kappa\nabla u) + \mathbf{w}\cdot\nabla u = f$ on the unit cube, discretised with 7-point finite differences, i.e. a nonsymmetric matrix with at most 7 nonzeros per row. We use Péclet numbers of 10 and 100 (resp. "mild" and "strong" convection), which give condition numbers of ca. $10^5$ and $10^7$ at the largest size. Unless stated otherwise the restart length is $m = 50$, the relative tolerance is $10^{-8}$, and the preconditioner is block Jacobi with one ILU(0) block per MPI rank, e.g. 64 blocks on a single node. Dr. Asante's earlier note (TN No. 2025-11) used $m = 30$ instead; the difference matters, see Sect. \@ref(results) and Tab. \@ref(tab:iters). # Setup {#setup} All runs used the `short` partition of larch: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 (96 cores each, 2.4 GHz base) and 768 GB of DDR5 per node, connected by HDR-200 InfiniBand in a non-blocking fat tree. We placed 64 MPI ranks per node with 3 OpenMP threads each, pinned with `--cpu-bind=cores`, and used Open MPI 4.1.6 with UCX 1.16 and GCC 13.2. The `MPI_Allreduce` latency for 8 B, measured with the OSU micro-benchmarks v7.4, grows from 2.1 µs on 2 nodes to 9.8 µs on 64 nodes, i.e. roughly as $\log_2 p$, as expected for a recursive-doubling algorithm. Nodes were allocated with `--exclusive` and `--switches=1@01:00:00` where possible, so most jobs ran within a single leaf switch; the 32- and 64-node runs necessarily span several. We report speed-up and parallel efficiency relative to the smallest run, \begin{equation} S(p) = \frac{T(p_0)}{T(p)}, \qquad E(p) = \frac{p_0\, S(p)}{p}, (\#eq:speedup) \end{equation} where $p_0 = 1$ node (192 cores) for strong scaling. For weak scaling we keep $n/p \approx 3.4 \times 10^6$ unknowns per node and report $E_w(p) = T(p_0)/T(p)$ instead, cf. Eq. \@ref(eq:speedup) with $S$ replaced by the time ratio. Note that $E$ can exceed 1 when the local problem starts to fit into the 384 MB of L3 cache per node, which happens at 32 nodes for $n = 2.0 \times 10^8$ (see below). # Results {#results} (ref:strong-cap) Strong scaling for $n = 2.0 \times 10^8$ (Pe = 100). Solid: p-GMRES; dashed: GMRES; grey: ideal. ```{r strong, fig.cap="(ref:strong-cap)", fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width="85%"} ggplot(res[kind == "strong"], aes(nodes, time_per_iter, linetype = solver)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = t_min, ymax = t_max), width = 0.05) + scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2", breaks = params$nodes) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "nodes", y = "time per iteration (s)") + theme_bw() ``` Fig. \@ref(fig:strong) shows that p-GMRES is no faster than GMRES up to 4 nodes, but on 64 nodes it reduces the time per iteration from 11.8 ms to 7.1 ms, i.e. by 40 %. The parallel efficiency at 64 nodes rises from 0.55 to 0.89 accordingly. This is consistent with the model of Ghysels et al. (2013, Eq. 12) and with the measurements of Sanan et al. [-@sanan2016pipelined] on a Cray XC40, although their speed-ups were larger (up to 2.5×) because the Aries network has a higher reduction latency than HDR InfiniBand. Is the extra cost of pipelining ever prohibitive? Not in our runs: the additional AXPY operations add approx. 6 % to the single-node time, which is within the run-to-run noise of ±4 %. Table: (\#tab:iters) Iterations to reach $\|r_k\|_2/\|b\|_2 < 10^{-8}$ for Pe = 100, by restart length. | nodes | GMRES(30) | GMRES(50) | p-GMRES(50) | |------:|----------:|----------:|------------:| | 1 | 412 | 298 | 301 | | 16 | 655 | 471 | 478 | | 64 | 803 | 560 | 571 | Tab. \@ref(tab:iters) shows the price in iterations. Block Jacobi weakens as the number of blocks grows (from 64 to 4,096), so all variants need more iterations at scale; p-GMRES needs 1–2 % more than GMRES because of the shifted basis, cf. Eqs. (3.4)–(3.6) in Ghysels et al. Increasing the restart length from 30 to 50 cuts iterations by approx. 30 % at every node count, at the cost of $50 \times 3.4 \times 10^6 \times 8\,\mathrm{B} \approx 1.4$ GB of extra basis storage per node, which is negligible on 768 GB nodes but not on the 256 GB nodes of the old `larch-legacy` partition. In total we ran `r nrow(res)` jobs, using approx. 9,800 node-hours. Two caveats apply. First, the runs at 32 and 64 nodes were done during the maintenance window on 2 Nov. 2026, when the rest of the machine was idle; on a busy system, network contention from other jobs typically adds 10–20 % to the reduction latency (cf. Fig. 7 in Chunduri et al. [-@chunduri2017runtime]), which would make pipelining *more* attractive, not less. Second, we did not tune the `UCX_TLS` and `UCX_RNDV_THRESH` settings, so the absolute numbers are probably pessimistic by a few percent. > In short: use p-GMRES on 16 nodes or more, and GMRES below that. The crossover moves to fewer nodes for smaller problems, e.g. ca. 8 nodes for $n = 5 \times 10^7$. # Weak scaling ```{r weak} #| fig.cap: "Weak-scaling efficiency $E_w(p)$ with $3.4 \\times 10^6$ unknowns per node." #| fig.width: 7 #| fig.height: 3.5 ggplot(res[kind == "weak"], aes(nodes, efficiency, colour = solver)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2", breaks = params$nodes) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.1)) + theme_bw() ``` Weak scaling is less flattering for both methods, since the iteration count grows like $\mathcal{O}(h^{-1})$ for this preconditioner, so the total time grows even at perfect per-iteration efficiency. Per iteration, p-GMRES keeps $E_w > 0.8$ up to 64 nodes vs. 0.61 for GMRES. A two-level preconditioner (e.g. the smoothed-aggregation AMG from fernsolve 2.3, cf. Sect. 4 of the user guide) would remove the growth in iterations; that is the subject of TN-2026-09. # Recommendations 1. Default to `gmres_pipelined()` when running on 16 or more nodes, and keep `gmres()` below that. The automatic choice in `fernsolve.krylov.solve(..., method="auto")` now does exactly this (v2.5.0, PR #1051). 2. Use $m = 50$ unless memory is tight. On the legacy nodes, $m = 30$ is a reasonable compromise. 3. Re-run this study once the H100 partition supports GPU-aware MPI reductions; Prof. Lindqvist's group expects that by Q2 2027. All scripts, raw timings and the `sbatch` files are archived at .[^repro] [^repro]: The archive also contains the exact Spack environment (`spack.lock`). Rebuilding it on another system should give identical binaries, modulo the CPU target. We have not tried this on ARM. # References {-}

--- {{< include _common.qmd >}} ## Summary {#sec-summary} ::: {.callout-important} ## Bottom line The regridded ensemble is fit for the detection-and-attribution work in WP3. Regridding changes the global-mean SST by **< 0.004 K** for every model (@tbl-regrid-error), the anomaly time series agree with the native-grid ones to within 0.01 K at every time step, and only `CanESM5` and `IPSL-CM6A-LR` need de-drifting (@sec-drift). ::: ## Data and models {#sec-data} We use monthly `tos` from the `historical` (1850–2014) and `ssp245`/`ssp585` (2015–2100) experiments of the five models in @tbl-models, three members each where available [@eyring2016; @oneill2016scenariomip]. Observations are HadISST [@rayner2003hadisst] and OISST v2.1 [@huang2021oisst, pp. 2923--2939], on their native $1^\circ$ and $0.25^\circ$ grids respectively. | Model | Ocean component | Native grid | Members | Ref. | |:--|:--|--:|:-:|---| | CanESM5 | NEMO3.4.1 (ORCA1) | ~1° | 3 | @swart2019canesm5 | | MPI-ESM1-2-HR | MPIOM1.63 (TP04) | 0.4° | 3 | @mueller2018mpiesm | | IPSL-CM6A-LR | NEMO-OPA (eORCA1) | ~1° | 3 | @boucher2020ipsl | | UKESM1-0-LL | NEMO3.6 (eORCA1) | ~1° | 2 | @sellar2019ukesm | | GFDL-CM4 | MOM6 | 0.25° | 1 | @held2019gfdlcm4 | : CMIP6 models in the ensemble refresh. "Members" counts realisations with complete historical *and* scenario output on our ESGF mirror as of 1 November 2026. {#tbl-models} ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-pipeline %%| fig-cap: The cmorph-pp chain. This report covers step 2 only. flowchart LR A[ESGF mirror
native tos] --> B(step 1: CMOR checks) B --> C(step 2: regrid + anomalies) C --> D[(THREDDS)] C --> E(step 3: bias correction) ``` ## Methods {#sec-methods} ### Regridding Fields are regridded with xESMF [@zhuang2023xesmf] using first-order conservative remapping, normalised by the unmasked fraction of each target cell (`conservative_normed`). For a target cell $k$ that overlaps source cells $i$ with overlap areas $a_{ik}$ and ocean mask $m_i \in \{0, 1\}$, $$ \hat T_k = \frac{\sum_i a_{ik}\, m_i\, T_i}{\sum_i a_{ik}\, m_i}, $$ {#eq-conservative} which, unlike plain conservative remapping, does not pull coastal cells towards zero. The global integral $\sum_k A_k \hat T_k$ is conserved exactly only if no target cell is partially masked; the residual error is what @tbl-regrid-error quantifies. ### Anomalies and drift {#sec-drift} Anomalies are taken relative to each member's 1981–2010 monthly climatology (@eq-anomaly). Drift is estimated from the parallel `piControl` segment with a least-squares quadratic fit $d(t) = a + b\,t + c\,t^2$ and subtracted when $|b| > 0.1\,\mathrm{K\,century^{-1}}$^[We tried a linear fit first. It under-corrects `IPSL-CM6A-LR`, whose drift slows down after ~200 years of spin-up.]. $$ T'(y, m) = T(y, m) - \frac{1}{30} \sum_{y'=1981}^{2010} T(y', m) $$ {#eq-anomaly} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} All runs were done on larch[^larch] as one Slurm array, one task per model and experiment: ```{.bash filename="jobs/submit_step2.sh"} sbatch --array=0-14%5 --partition=short --cpus-per-task=32 --mem=120G \ --time=04:00:00 --job-name=pp-step2 jobs/step2.sbatch ``` ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} > Weights for the 0.25° GFDL grid took 19 min to build on 32 cores; every later run reused them from `$CMORPH_WEIGHTS`. ::: :::: [^larch]: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 per node, 768 GB RAM. Regridding is memory-bound, so we used 32 of the 192 cores per task and packed six tasks onto each node. ## Results ### Regridding error ```{python} #| label: tbl-regrid-error #| tbl-cap: "Difference in 1981–2010 global-mean SST (K), regridded minus native, per model. Negative values mean the regridded field is cooler." import pandas as pd err = pd.read_parquet("results/regrid_error.parquet") err.style.format("{:+.4f}").background_gradient(cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.005, vmax=0.005) ``` ```{python} #| label: fig-gmsst #| fig-cap: Global-mean SST anomaly relative to 1981–2010, ensemble mean ± 1σ.

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
#SBATCH --job-name=covqc
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --array=1-96%24
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=01:30:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out

# coverage_qc.R -- per-sample coverage QC from mosdepth output (Mensah lab, varcall pipeline)
#
# Usage, one array task per sample (the sample list has one path prefix per line):
#   sbatch --export=ALL,SAMPLES=batches/2026_11.txt bin/coverage_qc.R
# or render the whole batch as an HTML report:
#   quarto render bin/coverage_qc.R -P batch:2026_11

#' # Coverage QC for a sequencing batch
#'
#' This script doubles as a `knitr::spin()` report: lines starting with `#'` are Markdown and `#|` lines are chunk options.

#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message:   FALSE
#| warning: no
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(glue)  
})
options(datatable.print.nrows = 20, warn = 1)

# fmt: markdown
# ## QC thresholds
#
# A sample **passes** if all of the following hold (agreed with the Genomics Core in Nov. 2025):
#
# | metric | threshold | why |
# |---|---|---|
# | median autosomal coverage | ≥ 30× | DeepVariant sensitivity drops quickly below ~25× (cf. Poplin et al. 2018) |
# | fraction of bases ≥ 20× | ≥ 0.90 | |
# | chrX / autosome ratio | consistent with the reported sex | catches sample swaps |
# | coverage CV | ≤ 0.35 | a high CV usually means GC bias or degraded DNA | 
#
# Samples between 20× and 30× are flagged `LOW` but still called; below 20× they `FAIL` and need re-sequencing.
# The coefficient of variation is computed over 1 kb bins as $\mathrm{CV} = \sigma / \mu$, excluding bins in the ENCODE blacklist (Amemiya et al. 2019).
THRESHOLDS <- list(
  median_cov  = 30,     # LOW below this
  hard_min    = 20,     # FAIL below this
  frac_ge20   = 0.90,
  cv_max      = 0.35,
  x_ratio_xx  = c(0.85, 1.15),
  x_ratio_xy  = c(0.40, 0.60)
)

# fmt: markdown
help_md <- r"---[
Per-sample coverage QC for **varcall** batches.

Reads `<prefix>.mosdepth.summary.txt` and `<prefix>.regions.bed.gz` (1 kb bins) for every sample listed in `$SAMPLES` and writes `<prefix>.covqc.tsv`. When run as a Slurm array job, task *i* processes line *i* of the sample list; otherwise all samples are processed one after the other, which takes about 40 s per 30× genome.

-   `SAMPLES`: path to the sample list (default `samples.txt`)
-   `SEX_TABLE`: optional TSV with columns `sample` and `sex` (`XX`/`XY`) from the sample sheet
]---"

# Batch summary, posted as a comment on the sequencing-run issue in GitLab.
# Placeholders are filled by glue::glue(), hence the {braces}.
# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence
summary_template <- r"(
## Coverage QC: batch {batch}

{n_pass} of {n_total} samples passed, {n_low} are `LOW` (20–30×) and {n_fail} `FAIL` (< 20×). Median coverage across the batch was {median_cov}× (IQR {iqr_lo}–{iqr_hi}×). Samples flagged `SEX_MISMATCH` must be checked against the sample sheet before anything else is done with them, since a swap always affects two samples.

{fail_table}

Re-sequencing requests go to the Core via the usual form, please link this issue. Plots: `{plot_path}`
)"

# Appended to each task's log so a single sample can be re-run outside Slurm.
# fmt: r
rerun_snippet <- "
source('bin/coverage_qc.R')
res <- qc_sample(prefix='%s',  sex = NA)
print(res[ , .(sample,median_cov,frac_ge20,cv,status)])
"



read_mosdepth <- function(prefix) {
  summ <- fread(paste0(prefix, ".mosdepth.summary.txt"))
  bins <- fread(paste0(prefix, ".regions.bed.gz"), col.names = c("chrom", "start", "end", "depth"))
  list(summary = summ, bins = bins)
}

qc_sample <- function(prefix, sex = NA_character_, thresholds = THRESHOLDS) {
  md <- read_mosdepth(prefix)
  auto <- md$bins[chrom %in% paste0("chr", 1:22)]
  med <- median(auto$depth)
  cv <- sd(auto$depth) / mean(auto$depth)
  frac20 <- mean(auto$depth >= 20)
  x_ratio <- median(md$bins[chrom == "chrX"]$depth) / med

# Contributing to varcall$
$
Thanks for helping out! `varcall` is the germline short-variant calling pipeline (FASTQ M-bM-^FM-^R aligned CRAM M-bM-^FM-^R gVCF M-bM-^FM-^R joint-called, filt
$
This document is for people *changing* the pipeline. If you only want to run it, read [README.md](README.md) and `docs/usage.md` instead.$
$
**Contents**$
$
1. [Ground rules](#ground-rules)$
2. [Development environment](#development-environment)$
3. [Tests](#tests)$
4. [Adding or updating a module](#adding-or-updating-a-module)$
5) [Commit messages and merge requests](#commit-messages-and-merge-requests)$
6) [Releasing](#releasing)$
$
Ground rules$
------------$
$
* Never commit patient-identifiable data. Test data under `tests/data/` is either synthetic or from the public **GIAB HG002** sample, downsampled to ~2M-CM-^W a
* All changes go through a merge request against `dev`; `main` only moves on releases. $
- Results must stay reproducible: an MR that changes any output VCF needs a justification in its description and an updated truth set (see [Tests](#tests)).$
*   Be kind in reviews. Most contributors are PhD students with a thesis to write.$
$
## Development environment  $
$
We use [pixi](https://pixi.sh) for Nextflow itself and the Python/R helpers, and containers (Apptainer on larch, Docker elsewhere) for the bioinformatics tools:
$
```bash$
git clone git@git.northfield.ac.uk:mensah-lab/varcall.git$
cd varcall$
pixi install            # nextflow, nf-test, python 3.12, R 4.4, pre-commit$
pixi run pre-commit install$
```$
$
On larch, do this on a login node but run anything heavier than `nf-test` in an interactive job (`salloc -p short -c 8 --mem=32G -t 2:00:00`). The login nodes k
$
> [!WARNING]$
> Do **not** keep the Apptainer cache in your home directory: home has a 50 GB quota and a single DeepVariant image is 6 GB. Put$
> `export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=/scratch/$USER/.apptainer` in your `~/.bashrc`.$
$
## Tests ##$
$
There are three layers of tests: $
$
1. **Unit tests** for the helper scripts (`pytest` for Python, `testthat` for R):$
$
   ```bash$
   pixi run pytest bin/tests -q$
   pixi run Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("bin/tests/testthat")'$
   ```$
2. **Module tests** with [nf-test](https://www.nf-test.com/), one per module under `modules/local/*/tests/`. Run all of them with `nf-test test --profile apptai
    ```bash$
    nf-test test modules/local/deepvariant/tests/main.nf.test --profile apptainer$
    ```$
3. **End-to-end** test on the GIAB subset. It takes ~25 min on 4 nodes and runs nightly in CI, but please run it yourself if you touch anything in `subworkflows
$
       sbatch --wait tests/e2e/run_e2e.sbatch$
       python tests/e2e/compare_to_truth.py results/e2e/HG002.vcf.gz --truth tests/data/HG002_chr20_truth.vcf.gz --min-f1 0.995$
$
   The comparison uses `hap.py`. An MR may lower SNV F1 by at most 0.001 and indel F1 by at most 0.003 without a discussion; anything more needs sign-off from t
$
### Making new test data$
$
If you need reads for a new region, downsample from the full 35M-CM-^W HG002 BAM rather than committing big files. To get a target coverage $c_t$ from an origin
$
```bash$
samtools view -b --subsample 0.057 --subsample-seed 42 HG002.GRCh38.35x.bam chr20:10000000-12000000 > HG002_chr20_2x.bam$
```$
$
Expected coverage after subsampling is $c_t$ only on average; for small regions check it with `mosdepth` and redraw with another seed if it is off by more than 
$
The `Makefile` in `tests/data/` regenerates everything (recipes must be indented with a tab, not spaces):$
$
```make$
HG002_chr20_2x.bam: $(SRC_BAM)$
^Isamtools view -b --subsample 0.057 --subsample-seed 42 $< chr20:10000000-12000000 > $@$
^Isamtools index $@$
```$
$

All the YAML parses as YAML 1.2 under Node's `yaml` package. That covers the YAML files, front matter, `yaml` fences and every `#|` block. The only warnings are for custom tags, which are there on purpose. I didn't run any formatter or change anything under `/workspace`.

A few files are deliberately unusual at the byte level:
- **`docker_compose.yml`:** uses CRLF line endings throughout.
- **`changelog.md`:** has mixed line endings; only its 2.0.0 section is CRLF.
- **`openapi.yaml`:** starts with a UTF-8 BOM.
- **`contributing.md`:** has real tab characters inside a Makefile code block.
